# facett_warehousedeck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-warehousedeck/0.1.10/facett_warehousedeck/

## Expand description

**facett-warehousedeck** — a multi-pane **dashboard over a lakehouse
warehouse**. It views the warehouse as **many components at once**: several
**3D graphs** (call graph, dependency graph, world-delta, release lineage,
SBOM/vuln) **plus** grids and charts, all visible simultaneously in a wall.

It is built **entirely from existing facett widgets** — it never reimplements
a viewer. Each pane is one of:
[ facett_graph3d::Graph3D](https://docs.rs/facett-graph3d/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_graph3d/struct.Graph3D.html) ·

[/](https://docs.rs/facett-grid/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_grid/struct.Grid.html)

`facett_grid::Grid`[·](https://docs.rs/facett-table/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_table/struct.Table.html)

`facett_table::Table`[, composed inside a](https://docs.rs/facett-plot/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_plot/struct.PlotView.html)

`facett_plot::PlotView`[. The deck is rendered in](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html)

`facett_core::FacetDeck`**Wall**mode (

[) so every pane (and thus several](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html#method.wall_ui)

`FacetDeck::wall_ui``Graph3D` instances) draws at once; a **Focus**mode falls back to the deck’s tabbed

[.](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html#method.ui)

`FacetDeck::ui`[§](https://docs.rs#engine-agnostic)Engine-agnostic

Like the rest of facett, this crate takes **data, not a catalog**: a host
(nornir’s viz) opens its Iceberg warehouse, reads each table, maps the rows to
a [ PaneData](https://docs.rs/enum.PaneData.html) view-model, and hands them in. This crate never depends on
iceberg/skade/nornir.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-registry-table--view-kind)The registry (table → view-kind)

[ WarehouseRegistry](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseRegistry.html) maps a

**table name**to the

[it should render as, so adding a table is one](https://docs.rs/enum.ViewKind.html)

`ViewKind``register(...)` line. The host queries the
registry to decide which [to build for a table; explicit join-panes (e.g. the call graph from](https://docs.rs/enum.PaneData.html)

`PaneData``call_edges`×`symbol_facts`) are added directly.[§](https://docs.rs#robot-testable)Robot-testable

[ WarehouseDeck](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseDeck.html) is itself a

[, so it drops into nornir’s viz and is headless-assertable.](https://docs.rs/trait.Facet.html)

`Facet`[exposes](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseDeck.html#method.state_json)

`WarehouseDeck::state_json``pane_count`,
per-kind counts (`graph3d_count`, `grid_count`, …), and a `panes` array
carrying each pane’s `nodes`/`edges`/`rows`/`series`, plus the composed deck
state (whose `trace.ran` lists `deck.wall:<title>` for every pane that drew).## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Chart](https://docs.rs/struct.ChartSpec.html)- Spec
- A chart view-model: named `(x, y)`series + the chart kind. Maps onto`PlotView`
- [Color32](https://docs.rs/struct.Color32.html)
- This format is used for space-efficient color representation (32 bits).
- [Graph](https://docs.rs/struct.GraphSpec.html)- Spec
- A 3D-graph view-model: `(label, color)`nodes + index edges + a layout. Maps directly onto`Graph3D::new`
- [Pane](https://docs.rs/struct.PaneInfo.html)- Info
- Per-pane metadata, mirrored into `state_json`for headless assertions.
- [Warehouse](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseDeck.html)- Deck
- A `FacetDeck``Facet`
- [Warehouse](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseRegistry.html)- Registry
- **table name →**— the registry that makes adding a table trivial. The host queries- `ViewKind`- `kind_for`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Deck](https://docs.rs/enum.DeckLayout.html)- Layout
- Deck render layout.
- [Graph](https://docs.rs/enum.GraphLayout.html)- Layout
- 3D placement strategies (positions are filled by `Graph3D::layout`
- [Pane](https://docs.rs/enum.PaneData.html)- Data
- The data a host hands per pane. The variant determines the widget; its
`ViewKind``PaneData::kind`
- [Plot](https://docs.rs/enum.PlotKind.html)- Kind
- [View](https://docs.rs/enum.ViewKind.html)- Kind
- How a warehouse table is rendered. The registry maps each table to one of
these; `PaneData`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Facet](https://docs.rs/trait.Facet.html)
- The facett **component contract**. Every facet — graph, map, pipeline, table, the ported nornir viewers — implements this, so consumers (korp, nornir, …) compose them uniformly*and*get headless robot-testing for free.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- A stable, bright-ish colour from a string (FNV-1a). Handy default node colour.

# sim_lib_pitch_namer_riemann - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-pitch-namer-riemann/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_pitch_namer_riemann/

## Expand description

Neo-Riemannian / functional triad naming for the SIM music libraries.

This crate implements the Riemannian naming school: it labels a triad by its
functional quality relative to its root, distinguishing a major triad (`T`,
upper-case for the major tonic function) from a minor triad (`t`,
lower-case). [ label_riemann](https://docs.rs/fn.label_riemann.html) rotates the pitch-class set so the root sits at
zero and matches the major or minor triad signature; non-triadic sets return

`None`.## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [label_](https://docs.rs/fn.label_riemann.html)- riemann
- Labels `mask`as a major (`T`) or minor (`t`) triad relative to its root.

# facett_security - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-security/0.1.10/facett_security/

## Expand description

**facett-security** — a software-supply-chain **security report** view: the
**verdict** (Pass / Warn / Block), the **findings** list (id · severity ·
package · advisory · fix) with **severity / EPSS / KEV** columns, and a
secondary **CVE / advisory** reference table. It is the UI *twin* of
[modgunn](https://codeberg.org/nordisk/modgunn)’s scan output — the gate that
decides whether an artifact may be served / promoted.

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-on-purpose-no-modgunn-dependency)Generic on purpose (no modgunn dependency)

facett MUST NOT couple to the modgunn crate. So this crate carries its **own**
plain, serializable structs — [ Verdict](https://docs.rs/enum.Verdict.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)

`Severity`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html)

`Finding`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)

`Artifact`[— whose shape](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityReport.html)

`SecurityReport`**mirrors**so a consumer (nornir-viz / holger-ui) maps the two

`modgunn::core`**1:1**with no glue:

| facett-security | modgunn::core |
|---|---|
| (Pass/Warn/Block)`Verdict` | `Decision`(Pass/Warn/Block) — same`Ord` |
| (Info…Critical)`Severity` | `Severity`(Info…Critical) — same`Ord` |
| `Finding``{id,severity,…}` | `Finding``{id,severity,summary}`(superset) |
| `Artifact` | `ArtifactRef` |
| `SecurityReport` | `Verdict`(the whole cacheable result) |

[ Finding](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html) is a

**superset**: modgunn’s three fields map straight in, and the richer scan columns the UI wants (

`package`, `advisory`, `fix`, `epss`, `kev`)
are optional, so a 1:1 mapper fills what it has and leaves the rest defaulted.[§](https://docs.rs#fc-compliance-the-component-contract)FC compliance (the component contract)

- **FC-1 / FC-3**— all observable state lives in one serializable- `SecurityState`- `Serialize`/- `Deserialize`/- `Clone`/- `PartialEq`), read back via- `SecurityView::state`
- **FC-2 / FC-9**— every input is a- `Msg`- `SecurityView::update`- `render`- `&self`that paints and- *returns*the- `Msg`- `Facet::ui`
- **FC-4**— the painted verdict pill emits an AccessKit node; every finding row / CVE row is a selectable, labelled, value-carrying node.
- **FC-5**— rows are keyed off the finding- **id**(a stable domain key), never a loop index.
- **FC-6**— pure egui + painter, renders headlessly (the deck robot path).
- **FC-7**— no ambient clock / RNG / animation: the scan time is an- *injected*host-stamped string (- `SecurityReport::scanned_at`
- **FC-8**— the view does no I/O;- `SecurityView::is_idle`- `SecurityView::update`- `Vec<Effect>`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Artifact](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)
- The artifact a verdict is about (content-addressed). Mirrors
`modgunn::core::ArtifactRef`.
- [Finding](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html)
- One thing the scanner found. `id`,`severity`,`summary`map straight from`modgunn::core::Finding`; the rest are the richer scan columns the UI shows (all optional, so a 1:1 mapper fills what it has).
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityReport.html)- Report
- The cacheable scan result: the verdict + its findings + the keys it was
computed against. The plain data a host hands the view; mirrors the whole of
`modgunn::core::Verdict`.
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityState.html)- State
- **All**observable state for the view (FC-1 / FC-3): the report plus the UI state (the drilled-in finding, the severity floor filter, and the zoom). Fully serializable so a caller reads it back at any frame boundary.
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityView.html)- View
- The `Facet``SecurityReport`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Effect](https://docs.rs/enum.Effect.html)
- Side work as data (FC-8). The view does no I/O, so this is uninhabited — it exists to make the “no pending effects” contract explicit and type-checked.
- [Msg](https://docs.rs/enum.Msg.html)
- Every input the view accepts (FC-2). The **only**legal way to mutate`SecurityState``Debug`+`Clone`.
- [Severity](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)
- Finding severity (declaration order = ascending, so the worst finding is the
`max()`). Mirrors`modgunn::core::Severity`.
- [Verdict](https://docs.rs/enum.Verdict.html)
- What a gate should DO with the artifact, given the findings. Declaration
order is the strictness order — `Pass < Warn < Block`— so folding many findings into one verdict is their`Ord::max``modgunn::core::Decision`relies on).

# facett_plandag - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-plandag/0.1.10/facett_plandag/

## Expand description

**facett-plandag** — a **metric-bearing operator DAG**: the Spark **SQL query
plan** / Databricks **Query Profile graph**. Each node carries a multi-line
**metric body** (time / memory / rows / spill); a **cost-heat** switch
(Time / Memory / Rows) fills nodes by relative cost; **WholeStageCodegen groups**
collapse into super-nodes; and an **AQE initial-vs-final** toggle flips between
the two plan versions. The four things the doc says no single facett graph had
at once.

It **composes** facett’s existing graph stack — exactly the documented “compose
`facett_graph`, paint our own” pattern:

- `facett_graph::DepGraphView`- **column layering**+- `facett_graph::draw_arrow`
- [`facett_pipeline::Status`] supplies the**themed node-status colour**.
- The pure, serializable `model`

[§](https://docs.rs#fc-contract)FC contract

- **Serializable state**(- `state_json`): the resolved graph (every node’s metric body + its- **cost-heat as DATA**), the active metric/version, the collapse set, the selection.
- `Msg`- `PlanDagView::update`
- **Render-proof**: the painter and- `state_json`both read from one- `model::resolve`

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use model::`- [CostMetric](https://docs.rs/model/enum.CostMetric.html);
- `pub use model::`- [Metrics](https://docs.rs/model/struct.Metrics.html);
- `pub use model::`- [OpStatus](https://docs.rs/model/enum.OpStatus.html);
- `pub use model::`- [PlanEdge](https://docs.rs/model/struct.PlanEdge.html);
- `pub use model::`- [PlanModel](https://docs.rs/model/struct.PlanModel.html);
- `pub use model::`- [PlanNode](https://docs.rs/model/struct.PlanNode.html);
- `pub use model::`- [PlanVersion](https://docs.rs/model/struct.PlanVersion.html);
- `pub use model::`- [Resolved](https://docs.rs/model/struct.Resolved.html);
- `pub use model::`- [ResolvedNode](https://docs.rs/model/struct.ResolvedNode.html);
- `pub use model::`- [resolve](https://docs.rs/model/fn.resolve.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html)
- The **engine-agnostic operator-plan model**— the neutral shape a host maps a Spark**SQL query plan**/ a Databricks**Query Profile graph**/ an**AQE adaptive plan**onto, and`PlanDagView``resolve`

# facett_helix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-helix/0.1.10/facett_helix/

## Expand description

**facett-helix** — the **TIME-HELIX DAG view**. A plan / dependency DAG rendered
as a **helix that advances ALONG a time axis**: each node is a plan item (idea /
task / test / crate) tied to a `system` (its angular lane / strand); the DAG winds
*forward through time* rather than spinning in place. Edges are **soft rounded
rubberband splines** (Catmull-Rom, elastic settle); coils can be **wound onto a
pin** (`wind`); many coils coexist in one scene with **inter-helix links**; an
**animated traverse** flies a time-cursor along the axis. GPU-rendered with the
emissive **bloom** lane reused from `facett-graph3d`.

[§](https://docs.rs#portability-contract-the-reason-this-crate-exists)Portability contract (the reason this crate exists)

[ model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html) +

[depend on](https://docs.rs/layout/index.html)

`layout`**nothing but**— no egui, no facett, no nornir/modgunn. They are the seam that

`serde` + `std``git mv`s into **ordning**. Only

[(this file) binds to facett’s](https://docs.rs/struct.HelixView.html)

`HelixView`[/egui/](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html)

`Facet``facett-graph3d`. Hosts
(nornir’s funnel, modgunn) just *populate*a

[through the](https://docs.rs/model/struct.Scene.html)

`model::Scene`[API; facett stays generic.](https://docs.rs/model/struct.PlanDag.html#method.add_idea)

`model::PlanDag::add_idea`[§](https://docs.rs#fc-contract)FC contract

- **Serializable state**(- `state_json`- `t`, angular lane, system) + the wind / level / cursor / tension — the picture asserted as DATA.
- `Msg`- `update`
- **Injected clock**(- `set_clock`- `Msg::Tick`
- **AccessKit**: each node rides into the tree as a queryable Button (FC-4).

# everruns_a2ui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-a2ui/0.17.3/everruns_a2ui/

## Expand description

A2UI component catalog and prompt generator for Everruns.

Produces system prompts that instruct LLMs to emit A2UI JSON component trees. The JSON is transported in ```a2ui fenced code blocks and rendered by the UI using native shadcn/ui primitives.

This crate is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_a2ui::{PromptOptions, default_catalog, generate_prompt};
let prompt = generate_prompt(default_catalog(), &PromptOptions::default());
assert!(prompt.contains("```a2ui"));
```
Ref: specs/a2ui.md
Ref: [https://github.com/google/a2ui](https://github.com/google/a2ui)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Catalog](https://docs.rs/struct.Catalog.html)
- A catalog describes the components an agent may emit.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentCategory.html)- Category
- One category of components in a catalog (e.g. “Layout”, “Forms”).
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentDef.html)- Def
- One component available to the agent.
- [Prompt](https://docs.rs/struct.PromptOptions.html)- Options
- Options for customizing the generated prompt.
- [PropDef](https://docs.rs/struct.PropDef.html)
- One prop of a component.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_catalog.html)- catalog
- The default A2UI catalog.
- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_prompt.html)- prompt
- Generate the default A2UI system prompt with standard options.
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_prompt.html)- prompt
- Build the full A2UI system prompt.

# everruns_openui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-openui/0.17.3/everruns_openui/

## Expand description

OpenUI component library and prompt generator for Everruns.

Rust reimplementation of the OpenUI component definitions and prompt generator. Produces system prompts that instruct LLMs to generate OpenUI Lang code.

The generated prompt is compatible with `@openuidev/react-lang` and `@openuidev/react-ui`
— the React runtime parses the LLM output and renders it into interactive components.

This crate is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_openui::{PromptOptions, default_library, generate_prompt};
let prompt = generate_prompt(default_library(), &PromptOptions::default());
assert!(prompt.contains("```openui"));
```
Ref: [https://github.com/thesysdev/openui](https://github.com/thesysdev/openui)

- Component definitions: packages/react-ui/src/genui-lib/
- Prompt generator: packages/react-lang/src/parser/prompt.ts
- Library/types: packages/react-lang/src/library.ts

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentDef.html)- Def
- A component definition.
Equivalent to TS `DefinedComponent`from`defineComponent()`.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentGroup.html)- Group
- A logical group of components for prompt organization.
- [Library](https://docs.rs/struct.Library.html)
- The full component library definition.
- [Prompt](https://docs.rs/struct.PromptOptions.html)- Options
- Options for customizing the generated prompt.
- [PropDef](https://docs.rs/struct.PropDef.html)
- A single prop/argument definition for a component.
Maps to a key in the TypeScript Zod schema’s `.shape`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_library.html)- library
- The default OpenUI library matching `@openuidev/react-ui`openuiChatLibrary. Ref: packages/react-ui/src/genui-lib/openuiChatLibrary.tsx
- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_prompt.html)- prompt
- Generate the default OpenUI system prompt with standard options.
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_prompt.html)- prompt
- Generate the complete OpenUI system prompt.

# athena_pipelines - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/athena-pipelines/3.26.3/athena_pipelines/

## Expand description

Portable Athena pipeline contracts and request-domain helpers.

This crate owns the declarative pipeline model that can be shared across the
server runtime, admin APIs, CLI/bootstrap loading, and future adapters
without depending on Actix or `AppState`.

The current scope covers:

- source/transform/sink pipeline DTOs,
- pipeline request payloads and template summaries,
- persisted template DTOs and record-to-runtime conversion helpers,
- pipeline template SQL adapters and step-log persistence helpers,
- request-independent pipeline execution orchestration behind runtime traits,
- database-backed template catalog loaders and list response contracts,
- YAML registry loading for named pipelines,
- validation and template/override resolution,
- template-name normalization and boot-template shadow policy helpers,
- gateway fetch-body construction and row alias rewriting.
- pipeline execution response contracts shared by runtime handlers and tests.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.ConditionEntry.html)- Entry
- A single equality condition in pipeline source configuration.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineDefinition.html)- Definition
- Full declarative pipeline definition used by templates and request merging.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineExecutionError.html)- Execution - Error
- Serializable per-row sink error returned from pipeline execution routes.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineExecutionResponse.html)- Execution - Response
- Serializable success envelope returned from `/pipelines`and`/pipelines/simulate`.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineFetchFailure.html)- Fetch - Failure
- Structured source-fetch failure returned by the runtime adapter.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineRequest.html)- Request
- Pipeline execution request with an optional named template and inline overrides.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineRunContext.html)- RunContext
- Runtime context needed by the portable pipeline runner.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineRunFetchFailure.html)- RunFetch - Failure
- Failed pipeline-run result when the source fetch cannot complete.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineRunSuccess.html)- RunSuccess
- Successful pipeline-run result returned by the portable runner.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineStepLogEntry.html)- Step - LogEntry
- One pipeline step-log row emitted for the `source`,`transform`, or`sink`stage.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineTemplateCandidate.html)- Template - Candidate
- Portable template candidate used when merging runtime-managed templates with boot registry entries.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineTemplateListResponse.html)- Template - List - Response
- Response envelope returned by `GET /pipelines/templates`.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineTemplateRecord.html)- Template - Record
- Portable persisted pipeline template record shared by SQL adapters and API responses.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineTemplateSummary.html)- Template - Summary
- Summary returned when listing named pipeline templates.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/struct.PipelineTemplateSummaryMerge.html)- Template - Summary - Merge
- Result of merging boot templates with runtime-provided templates.
- [Save](https://docs.rs/struct.SavePipelineTemplateRequest.html)- Pipeline - Template - Request
- Request body for saving a managed pipeline template through admin surfaces.
- [Sink](https://docs.rs/struct.SinkConfig.html)- Config
- Sink-stage configuration for Athena pipelines.
- [Source](https://docs.rs/struct.SourceConfig.html)- Config
- Source stage configuration for Athena pipelines.
- [Transform](https://docs.rs/struct.TransformConfig.html)- Config
- Transform-stage configuration for grouped or cumulative fetch post-processing.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/enum.PipelineRunOutcome.html)- RunOutcome
- Outcome returned by the portable pipeline runner.
- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/enum.PipelineTemplateCatalogError.html)- Template - Catalog - Error
- Errors returned while loading database-backed pipeline templates for runtime use.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/trait.PipelineRuntime.html)- Runtime
- Runtime port used by the portable pipeline runner to fetch source rows and write sink rows.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [apply_](https://docs.rs/fn.apply_column_aliases.html)- column_ - aliases
- Rewrites fetched row keys according to configured sink aliases.
- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_fetch_body.html)- fetch_ - body
- Builds the gateway-style fetch JSON body for a pipeline source/transform pair.
- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_template_summary.html)- template_ - summary
- Builds the API-facing template summary for a named pipeline definition.
- [delete_](https://docs.rs/fn.delete_pipeline_template_by_name.html)- pipeline_ - template_ - by_ - name
- Deletes a managed pipeline template by name and returns the removed record, if present.
- [ensure_](https://docs.rs/fn.ensure_pipeline_step_log_table.html)- pipeline_ - step_ - log_ - table
- Ensures the pipeline step-log table exists on the logging Postgres database.
- [ensure_](https://docs.rs/fn.ensure_pipeline_template_table.html)- pipeline_ - template_ - table
- Ensures the managed pipeline-template catalog exists on the logging Postgres database.
- [execute_](https://docs.rs/fn.execute_pipeline_run.html)- pipeline_ - run
- Executes the portable fetch -> transform -> sink pipeline flow using runtime-provided I/O.
- [get_](https://docs.rs/fn.get_pipeline_template_by_name.html)- pipeline_ - template_ - by_ - name
- Loads a managed pipeline template by name using case-insensitive matching.
- [insert_](https://docs.rs/fn.insert_pipeline_step_log.html)- pipeline_ - step_ - log
- Persists a pipeline step-log row. Callers typically spawn this asynchronously from the route.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/fn.list_pipeline_templates.html)- pipeline_ - templates
- Lists every managed pipeline template sorted case-insensitively by name.
- [load_](https://docs.rs/fn.load_pipeline_definition_map.html)- pipeline_ - definition_ - map
- Loads the database-backed template definition map used by pipeline reference resolution.
- [load_](https://docs.rs/fn.load_pipeline_template_records.html)- pipeline_ - template_ - records
- Loads persisted pipeline template records from the optional logging pool.
- [load_](https://docs.rs/fn.load_pipeline_template_summary_merge.html)- pipeline_ - template_ - summary_ - merge
- Loads the merged template catalog used by `GET /pipelines/templates`.
- [load_](https://docs.rs/fn.load_registry_from_path.html)- registry_ - from_ - path
- Loads named pipeline definitions from a YAML file into a registry map.
- [merge_](https://docs.rs/fn.merge_template_summaries.html)- template_ - summaries
- Merges boot-registry templates with runtime-provided templates.
- [normalize_](https://docs.rs/fn.normalize_pipeline_template_name.html)- pipeline_ - template_ - name
- Normalizes a pipeline template name for route and admin request handling.
- [pipeline_](https://docs.rs/fn.pipeline_definition_from_value.html)- definition_ - from_ - value
- Parses and validates a pipeline definition from arbitrary JSON.
- [pipeline_](https://docs.rs/fn.pipeline_definition_map_from_records.html)- definition_ - map_ - from_ - records
- Builds the named-definition lookup map used by runtime pipeline resolution.
- [pipeline_](https://docs.rs/fn.pipeline_template_name_conflicts_with_registry.html)- template_ - name_ - conflicts_ - with_ - registry
- Returns whether a runtime-managed template name would shadow a boot-registry template.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_client_name.html)- client_ - name
- Picks the explicit pipeline client override or falls back to the request client.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_definition.html)- definition
- Resolves a request body into the effective pipeline definition.
- [runtime_](https://docs.rs/fn.runtime_template_candidates_from_records.html)- template_ - candidates_ - from_ - records
- Converts persisted records into runtime template candidates for summary merging.
- [upsert_](https://docs.rs/fn.upsert_pipeline_template.html)- pipeline_ - template
- Inserts or updates a managed pipeline template and returns the stored record.
- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_pipeline_definition.html)- pipeline_ - definition
- Validates that the minimum required pipeline fields are present.

# ic-cdk-macros 0.20.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ic-cdk-macros/0.20.2

# ic-cdk-macros

This crate contains a collection of procedural macros that are utilized within the `ic-cdk` crate.

The macros are re-exported in `ic-cdk`, and you can find their documentation [there](https://docs.rs/ic-cdk/latest/ic_cdk).

The macros fall into two categories:

- To register functions as canister entry points
- To export Candid definitions

## Register functions as canister entry points

These macros are directly related to the [Internet Computer Specification](https://internetcomputer.org/docs/current/references/ic-interface-spec#entry-points).

## Export Candid definitions

Check [Generating Candid files for Rust canisters](https://internetcomputer.org/docs/current/developer-docs/backend/candid/generating-candid/) for more details.

---

# ic-cdk-macros 0.20.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ic-cdk-macros/latest/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# candid 0.10.31 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/candid/^0.10.24

# Candid

[Candid](https://github.com/dfinity/candid/tree/master/spec/Candid.md) is an interface description language (IDL) for interacting with *canisters* (also known as *services* or *actors*) running on the Internet Computer.

The Candid crate is a serialization/deserialization library for Candid. You can seamlessly convert between Rust values and Candid in both binary and text format.

# Usage

See [the docs here](https://docs.rs/candid).

---

# darling 0.23.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/darling/^0.23.0

# Darling

`darling` is a crate for proc macro authors, which enables parsing attributes into structs. It is heavily inspired by `serde` both in its internals and in its API.

# Benefits

- Easy and declarative parsing of macro input - make your proc-macros highly controllable with minimal time investment.
- Great validation and errors, no work required. When users of your proc-macro make a mistake, `darling`makes sure they get error markers at the right place in their source, and provides "did you mean" suggestions for misspelled fields.

# Usage

`darling` provides a set of traits which can be derived or manually implemented.

- `FromMeta`is used to extract values from a meta-item in an attribute. Implementations are likely reusable for many libraries, much like- `FromStr`or- `serde::Deserialize`. Trait implementations are provided for primitives, some std types, and some- `syn`types.
- `FromDeriveInput`is implemented or derived by each proc-macro crate which depends on- `darling`. This is the root for input parsing; it gets access to the identity, generics, and visibility of the target type, and can specify which attribute names should be parsed or forwarded from the input AST.
- `FromField`is implemented or derived by each proc-macro crate which depends on- `darling`. Structs deriving this trait will get access to the identity (if it exists), type, and visibility of the field.
- `FromVariant`is implemented or derived by each proc-macro crate which depends on- `darling`. Structs deriving this trait will get access to the identity and contents of the variant, which can be transformed the same as any other- `darling`input.
- `FromAttributes`is a lower-level version of the more-specific- `FromDeriveInput`,- `FromField`, and- `FromVariant`traits. Structs deriving this trait get a meta-item extractor and error collection which works for any syntax element, including traits, trait items, and functions. This is useful for non-derive proc macros.

## Additional Modules

- `darling::ast`provides generic types for representing the AST.
- `darling::usage`provides traits and functions for determining where type parameters and lifetimes are used in a struct or enum.
- `darling::util`provides helper types with special- `FromMeta`implementations, such as- `PathList`.

# Example

```
use ;
```
The above code will then be able to parse this input:

```
/// A doc comment which will be available in `MyTraitOpts::attrs`.
;
```
# Attribute Macros

Non-derive attribute macros are supported.
To parse arguments for attribute macros, derive `FromMeta` on the argument receiver type, then use `darling::ast::NestedMeta::parse_meta_list` to convert the arguments `TokenStream` to a `Vec<NestedMeta>`, then pass that to the derived `from_list` method on your argument receiver type.
This will produce a normal `darling::Result<T>` that can be used the same as a result from parsing a `DeriveInput`.

## Macro Code

```
use ;
use NestedMeta;
use ItemFn;
use TokenStream;
```
## Consuming Code

```
use your_attr;
```
# Features

Darling's features are built to work well for real-world projects.

- **Defaults**: Supports struct- and field-level defaults, using the same path syntax as- `serde`. Additionally,- `Option<T>`and- `darling::util::Flag`fields are innately optional; you don't need to declare- `#[darling(default)]`for those.
- **Field Renaming**: Fields can have different names in usage vs. the backing code.
- **Auto-populated fields**: Structs deriving- `FromDeriveInput`and- `FromField`can declare properties named- `ident`,- `vis`,- `ty`,- `attrs`, and- `generics`to automatically get copies of the matching values from the input AST.- `FromDeriveInput`additionally exposes- `data`to get access to the body of the deriving type, and- `FromVariant`exposes- `fields`.- **Transformation of forwarded attributes**: You can add- `#[darling(with=path)]`to the- `attrs`field to use a custom function to transform the forwarded attributes before they're provided to your struct. The function signature is- `fn(Vec<Attribute>) -> darling::Result<T>`, where- `T`is the type you declared for the- `attrs`field. Returning an error from this function will propagate with all other parsing errors.

- **Mapping function**: Use- `#[darling(map="path")]`or- `#[darling(and_then="path")]`to specify a function that runs on the result of parsing a meta-item field. This can change the return type, which enables you to parse to an intermediate form and convert that to the type you need in your struct.
- **Skip fields**: Use- `#[darling(skip)]`to mark a field that shouldn't be read from attribute meta-items.
- **Multiple-occurrence fields**: Use- `#[darling(multiple)]`on a- `Vec`field to allow that field to appear multiple times in the meta-item. Each occurrence will be pushed into the- `Vec`.
- **Span access**: Use- `darling::util::SpannedValue`in a struct to get access to that meta item's source code span. This can be used to emit warnings that point at a specific field from your proc macro. In addition, you can use- `darling::Error::write_errors`to automatically get precise error location details in most cases.
- **"Did you mean" suggestions**: Compile errors from derived darling trait impls include suggestions for misspelled fields.
- **Struct flattening**: Use- `#[darling(flatten)]`to remove one level of structure when presenting your meta item to users. Fields that are not known to the parent struct will be forwarded to the- `flatten`field.
- **Custom shorthand**: Use- `#[darling(from_word = ...)]`on a struct or enum to override how a simple word is interpreted. By default, it is an error for your macro's user to fail to specify the fields of your struct, but with this you can choose to instead produce a set of default values. This takes either a path or a closure whose signature matches- `FromMeta::from_word`.
- **Custom handling for missing fields**: When a field is not present and- `#[darling(default)]`is not used, derived impls will call- `FromMeta::from_none`on that field's type to try and get the fallback value for the field. Usually, there is not a fallback value, so a missing field error is generated.- `Option<T: FromMeta>`uses this to make options optional without requiring- `#[darling(default)]`declarations, and structs and enums can use this themselves with- `#[darling(from_none = ...)]`. This takes either a path or a closure whose signature matches- `FromMeta::from_none`.
- **Generate**: When deriving- `syn::parse::Parse`impl- `FromMeta`, add- `#[darling(derive_syn_parse)]`to also generate an impl of the- `Parse`trait.

## Shape Validation

Some proc-macros only work on structs, while others need enums whose variants are either unit or newtype variants.
Darling makes this sort of validation extremely simple.
On the receiver that derives `FromDeriveInput`, add `#[darling(supports(...))]` and then list the shapes that your macro should accept.

| Name | Description |
|---|---|
| `any` | Accept anything |
| `struct_any` | Accept any struct |
| `struct_named` | Accept structs with named fields, e.g. `struct Example { field: String }` |
| `struct_newtype` | Accept newtype structs, e.g. `struct Example(String)` |
| `struct_tuple` | Accept tuple structs, e.g. `struct Example(String, String)` |
| `struct_unit` | Accept unit structs, e.g. `struct Example;` |
| `enum_any` | Accept any enum |
| `enum_named` | Accept enum variants with named fields |
| `enum_newtype` | Accept newtype enum variants |
| `enum_tuple` | Accept tuple enum variants |
| `enum_unit` | Accept unit enum variants |

Each one is additive, so listing `#[darling(supports(struct_any, enum_newtype))]` would accept all structs and any enum where every variant is a newtype variant.

This can also be used when deriving `FromVariant`, without the `enum_` prefix.

---

# proc-macro2 1.0.106 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/proc-macro2/^1.0.106

# proc-macro2

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler's `proc_macro` crate.
This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

## Usage

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you'll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to propagate
parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

## Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable compiler
API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not exposed by
proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly compiler,
the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to rustc. We will
polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As these are unstable APIs
that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of proc-macro2 may make breaking
changes to them at any time.

```
RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build
```
Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

---

# quote 1.0.46 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/quote/^1

# Rust Quasi-Quoting

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/quote/1.0/quote/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller's crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text editor
or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor's brace matching, syntax
highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than compiling
that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass it around,
mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens to compile into
the macro caller's crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Syntax

The quote crate provides a [ quote!](https://docs.rs/quote/1.0/quote/macro.quote.html) macro within which you can write Rust code
that gets packaged into a

[and can be treated as data. You should think of](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0/proc_macro2/struct.TokenStream.html)

`TokenStream``TokenStream` as representing a fragment of Rust source code.Within the `quote!` macro, interpolation is done with `#var`. Any type
implementing the [ quote::ToTokens](https://docs.rs/quote/1.0/quote/trait.ToTokens.html) trait can be interpolated. This includes
most Rust primitive types as well as most of the syntax tree types from

[.](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)

`syn````
let tokens = quote! ;
```
## Repetition

Repetition is done using `#(...)*` or `#(...),*` similar to `macro_rules!`. This
iterates through the elements of any variable interpolated within the repetition
and inserts a copy of the repetition body for each one. The variables in an
interpolation may be a `Vec`, slice, `BTreeSet`, or any `Iterator`.

- `#(#var)*`— no separators
- `#(#var),*`— the character before the asterisk is used as a separator
- `#( struct #var; )*`— the repetition can contain other things
- `#( #k => println!("{}", #v), )*`— even multiple interpolations

Note that there is a difference between `#(#var ,)*` and `#(#var),*`—the latter
does not produce a trailing comma. This matches the behavior of delimiters in
`macro_rules!`.

## Returning tokens to the compiler

The `quote!` macro evaluates to an expression of type
`proc_macro2::TokenStream`. Meanwhile Rust procedural macros are expected to
return the type `proc_macro::TokenStream`.

The difference between the two types is that `proc_macro` types are entirely
specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a
procedural macro, while `proc_macro2` types may exist anywhere including tests
and non-macro code like main.rs and build.rs. This is why even the procedural
macro ecosystem is largely built around `proc_macro2`, because that ensures the
libraries are unit testable and accessible in non-macro contexts.

There is a [ From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/convert/trait.From.html)-conversion in both directions so returning the output of

`quote!` from a procedural macro usually looks like `tokens.into()` or
`proc_macro::TokenStream::from(tokens)`.## Examples

### Combining quoted fragments

Usually you don't end up constructing an entire final `TokenStream` in one
piece. Different parts may come from different helper functions. The tokens
produced by `quote!` themselves implement `ToTokens` and so can be interpolated
into later `quote!` invocations to build up a final result.

```
let type_definition = quote! ;
let methods = quote! ;
let tokens = quote! ;
```
### Constructing identifiers

Suppose we have an identifier `ident` which came from somewhere in a macro
input and we need to modify it in some way for the macro output. Let's consider
prepending the identifier with an underscore.

Simply interpolating the identifier next to an underscore will not have the
behavior of concatenating them. The underscore and the identifier will continue
to be two separate tokens as if you had written `_ x`.

```
// incorrect
quote!
```
The solution is to build a new identifier token with the correct value. As this
is such a common case, the `format_ident!` macro provides a convenient utility
for doing so correctly.

```
let varname = format_ident!;
quote!
```
Alternatively, the APIs provided by Syn and proc-macro2 can be used to directly
build the identifier. This is roughly equivalent to the above, but will not
handle `ident` being a raw identifier.

```
let concatenated = format!;
let varname = new;
quote!
```
### Making method calls

Let's say our macro requires some type specified in the macro input to have a
constructor called `new`. We have the type in a variable called `field_type` of
type `syn::Type` and want to invoke the constructor.

```
// incorrect
quote!
```
This works only sometimes. If `field_type` is `String`, the expanded code
contains `String::new()` which is fine. But if `field_type` is something like
`Vec<i32>` then the expanded code is `Vec<i32>::new()` which is invalid syntax.
Ordinarily in handwritten Rust we would write `Vec::<i32>::new()` but for macros
often the following is more convenient.

```
quote!
```
This expands to `<Vec<i32>>::new()` which behaves correctly.

A similar pattern is appropriate for trait methods.

```
quote!
```
## Hygiene

Any interpolated tokens preserve the `Span` information provided by their
`ToTokens` implementation. Tokens that originate within a `quote!` invocation
are spanned with [ Span::call_site()](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0/proc_macro2/struct.Span.html#method.call_site).

A different span can be provided explicitly through the [ quote_spanned!](https://docs.rs/quote/1.0/quote/macro.quote_spanned.html)
macro.

## Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through [prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease)
before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated code it is
convenient for a human to read and debug.

Be aware that no kind of hygiene or span information is retained when tokens are written to a file; the conversion from tokens to source code is lossy.

Example usage in build.rs:

```
let output = quote! ;
let syntax_tree = parse2.unwrap;
let formatted = unparse;
let out_dir = var_os.unwrap;
let dest_path = new.join;
write.unwrap;
```

---

# syn 2.0.118 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/syn/^2

# Parser for Rust source code

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user's code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

## Resources

The best way to learn about procedural macros is by writing some. Consider
working through [this procedural macro workshop](https://github.com/dtolnay/proc-macro-workshop) to get familiar with
the different types of procedural macros. The workshop contains relevant links
into the Syn documentation as you work through each project.

## Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary Rust
function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of the trait
we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user's code, the Rust
compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We get to execute
arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those tokens, then hand some
tokens back to the compiler to compile into the user's crate.

```
[]
 = "2.0"
 = "1.0"
[]
 = true
```
```
use TokenStream;
use quote;
use ;
```
The [ heapsize](https://docs.rs/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation of a
derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an estimate
of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data structures
in their program.

```
```
## Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler's error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a procedural
macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in Syn are able to
trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `std::thread::Thread`
```
## Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://docs.rs/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed using
Syn's parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static!
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
## Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild) crate
to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors detected by
the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the macro. Such tests
help avoid regressions from later refactors that mistakenly make an error no
longer trigger or be less helpful than it used to be.

## Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro, run
`cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of your own
test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last argument is
the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust's new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

## Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Proc macro shim

Syn operates on the token representation provided by the [proc-macro2](https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/1.0/proc_macro2/) crate
from crates.io rather than using the compiler's built in proc-macro crate
directly. This enables code using Syn to execute outside of the context of a
procedural macro, such as in unit tests or build.rs, and we avoid needing
incompatible ecosystems for proc macros vs non-macro use cases.

In general all of your code should be written against proc-macro2 rather than
proc-macro. The one exception is in the signatures of procedural macro entry
points, which are required by the language to use `proc_macro::TokenStream`.

The proc-macro2 crate will automatically detect and use the compiler's data structures when a procedural macro is active.

# ic-cdk-macros

This crate contains a collection of procedural macros that are utilized within the `ic-cdk` crate.

The macros are re-exported in `ic-cdk`, and you can find their documentation [there](https://docs.rs/ic-cdk/latest/ic_cdk).

The macros fall into two categories:

- To register functions as canister entry points
- To export Candid definitions

## Register functions as canister entry points

These macros are directly related to the [Internet Computer Specification](https://internetcomputer.org/docs/current/references/ic-interface-spec#entry-points).

## Export Candid definitions

Check [Generating Candid files for Rust canisters](https://internetcomputer.org/docs/current/developer-docs/backend/candid/generating-candid/) for more details.

# ic-cdk-macros 0.18.0-alpha.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ic-cdk-macros/0.18.0-alpha.1

# ic-cdk-macros

This crate contains a collection of procedural macros that are utilized within the `ic-cdk` crate.

The macros are re-exported in `ic-cdk`, and you can find their documentation [there](https://docs.rs/ic-cdk/latest/ic_cdk).

The macros fall into two categories:

- To register functions as canister entry points
- To export Candid definitions

## Register functions as canister entry points

These macros are directly related to the [Internet Computer Specification](https://internetcomputer.org/docs/current/references/ic-interface-spec#entry-points).

## Export Candid definitions

Check [Generating Candid files for Rust canisters](https://internetcomputer.org/docs/current/developer-docs/backend/candid/generating-candid/) for more details.

---

# ic-cdk-macros

**Internet Computer Canister Development Kit**

This crate provides attribute macros, with which you can annotate regular rust functions to be public interfaces of a canister.

# candid 0.10.31 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/candid/0.10.31

# Candid

[Candid](https://github.com/dfinity/candid/tree/master/spec/Candid.md) is an interface description language (IDL) for interacting with *canisters* (also known as *services* or *actors*) running on the Internet Computer.

The Candid crate is a serialization/deserialization library for Candid. You can seamlessly convert between Rust values and Candid in both binary and text format.

# Usage

See [the docs here](https://docs.rs/candid).

---

# anyhow - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/anyhow/^1.0/

## Expand description

This library provides [ anyhow::Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html), a trait object based error
type for easy idiomatic error handling in Rust applications.

[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Use `Result<T, anyhow::Error>`, or equivalently`anyhow::Result<T>`, as the return type of any fallible function.Within the function, use `?`to easily propagate any error that implements the`std::error::Error``use anyhow::Result; fn get_cluster_info() -> Result<ClusterMap> { let config = std::fs::read_to_string("cluster.json")?; let map: ClusterMap = serde_json::from_str(&config)?; Ok(map) }`
-
Attach context to help the person troubleshooting the error understand where things went wrong. A low-level error like “No such file or directory” can be annoying to debug without more context about what higher level step the application was in the middle of. `use anyhow::{Context, Result}; fn main() -> Result<()> { ... it.detach().context("Failed to detach the important thing")?; let content = std::fs::read(path) .with_context(|| format!("Failed to read instrs from {}", path))?; ... }``Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)`
-
Downcasting is supported and can be by value, by shared reference, or by mutable reference as needed. `// If the error was caused by redaction, then return a // tombstone instead of the content. match root_cause.downcast_ref::<DataStoreError>() { Some(DataStoreError::Censored(_)) => Ok(Poll::Ready(REDACTED_CONTENT)), None => Err(error), }`
-
If using Rust ≥ 1.65, a backtrace is captured and printed with the error if the underlying error type does not already provide its own. In order to see backtraces, they must be enabled through the environment variables described in `std::backtrace`- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only errors to have backtraces, set `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only panics to have backtraces, set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`and`RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`.

- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
-
Anyhow works with any error type that has an impl of `std::error::Error`, including ones defined in your crate. We do not bundle a`derive(Error)`macro but you can write the impls yourself or use a standalone macro like[thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror).`use thiserror::Error; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum FormatError { #[error("Invalid header (expected {expected:?}, got {found:?})")] InvalidHeader { expected: String, found: String, }, #[error("Missing attribute: {0}")] MissingAttribute(String), }`
-
One-off error messages can be constructed using the `anyhow!`macro, which supports string interpolation and produces an`anyhow::Error`.`return Err(anyhow!("Missing attribute: {}", missing));`A `bail!`macro is provided as a shorthand for the same early return.`bail!("Missing attribute: {}", missing);`

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

In no_std mode, almost all of the same API is available and works the same way. To depend on Anyhow in no_std mode, disable our default enabled “std” feature in Cargo.toml. A global allocator is required.

```
[dependencies]
anyhow = { version = "1.0", default-features = false }
```
With versions of Rust older than 1.81, no_std mode may require an additional
`.map_err(Error::msg)` when working with a non-Anyhow error type inside a
function that returns Anyhow’s error type, as the trait that `?`-based error
conversions are defined by is only available in std in those old versions.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [anyhow](https://docs.rs/macro.anyhow.html)as format_err;

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [anyhow](https://docs.rs/macro.anyhow.html)
- Construct an ad-hoc error from a string or existing non-`anyhow`error value.
- [bail](https://docs.rs/macro.bail.html)
- Return early with an error.
- [ensure](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html)
- Return early with an error if a condition is not satisfied.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.Chain.html)
- Iterator of a chain of source errors.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- The `Error`type, a wrapper around a dynamic error type.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Context](https://docs.rs/trait.Context.html)
- Provides the `context`method for`Result`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [Ok](https://docs.rs/fn.Ok.html)
- Equivalent to `Ok::<_, anyhow::Error>(value)`.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- `Result<T, Error>`

---

# binread - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/binread/^2.2/

## Expand description

A Rust crate for helping parse binary data using ✨macro magic✨.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
#[derive(BinRead)]
#[br(magic = b"DOG", assert(name.len() != 0))]
struct Dog {
    bone_pile_count: u8,
    #[br(big, count = bone_pile_count)]
    bone_piles: Vec<u16>,
    #[br(align_before = 0xA)]
    name: NullString
}
let mut reader = Cursor::new(b"DOG\x02\x00\x01\x00\x12\0\0Rudy\0");
let dog: Dog = reader.read_ne().unwrap();
assert_eq!(dog.bone_piles, &[0x1, 0x12]);
assert_eq!(dog.name.into_string(), "Rudy")
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-basics)The Basics

At the core of `binread` is the [ BinRead](https://docs.rs/trait.BinRead.html) trait. It defines how to read
a type from bytes and is already implemented for most primitives and simple collections.

```
use binread::{BinRead, io::Cursor};
let mut reader = Cursor::new(b"\0\0\0\x01");
let val = u32::read(&mut reader).unwrap();
```
However, [ read](https://docs.rs/trait.BinRead.html#method.read) is intentionally simple and, as a result, doesn’t even
allow you to configure the byte order. For that you need

[which, while more powerful, isn’t exactly ergonomics.](https://docs.rs/trait.BinRead.html#tymethod.read_options)

`read_options`So, as a balance between ergonomics and configurability you have the [ BinReaderExt](https://docs.rs/trait.BinReaderExt.html)
trait. It is an extension for readers to allow for you to directly read any BinRead types from
any reader.

Example:

```
use binread::{BinReaderExt, io::Cursor};
let mut reader = Cursor::new(b"\x00\x0A");
let val: u16 = reader.read_be().unwrap();
assert_eq!(val, 10);
```
It even works for tuples and arrays of BinRead types for up to size 32.

[§](https://docs.rs#derive-macro)Derive Macro

The most significant feature of binread is its ability to use the Derive macro to
implement [ BinRead](https://docs.rs/trait.BinRead.html) for your own types. This allows you to replace repetitive
imperative code with declarative struct definitions for your binary data parsing.

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-derive-example)Basic Derive Example

```
#[derive(BinRead)]
struct MyType {
    first: u32,
    second: u32
}
// Also works with tuple types!
#[derive(BinRead)]
struct MyType2(u32, u32);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)Attributes

The BinRead derive macro uses attributes in order to allow for more complicated parsers. For
example you can use `big` or `little` at either the struct-level or the field-level in order
to override the byte order of values.

```
#[derive(BinRead)]
#[br(little)]
struct MyType (
    #[br(big)] u32, // will be big endian
    u32, // will be little endian
);
```
The order of precedence is: (from highest to lowest)

- Field-level
- Variant-level (for enums)
- Top-level
- Configured (i.e. what endianess was passed in)
- Native endianess

For a list of attributes see the [ attribute](https://docs.rs/attribute/index.html) module

[§](https://docs.rs#generics)Generics

The BinRead derive macro also allows for generic parsing. That way you can build up higher-level parsers that can have their type swapped out to allow greater reuse of code.

```
#[derive(BinRead)]
struct U32CountVec<T: BinRead<Args=()>> {
    count: u32,
    #[br(count = count)]
    data: Vec<T>,
}
```
In order to parse generically, we have to (in some way) bound `Args`. The easiest way to do
this is to bound `<T as BinRead>::Args` to `()` (no arguments), however it is also possible to
either accept a specific set of arguments or be generic over the given arguments.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `const_generics`- Change array- `BinRead`
- `std`- Disable this feature to enable- `no_std`support, on by default

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [attribute](https://docs.rs/attribute/index.html)
- A documentation-only module for the possible directives used in `#[br]`and`#[binread]`attributes.
- [endian](https://docs.rs/endian/index.html)
- An enum to represent what endianness to read as
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error types and internal error handling functions
- [file_](https://docs.rs/file_ptr/index.html)- ptr
- A wrapper type for representing a layer of indirection within a file.
- [helpers](https://docs.rs/helpers/index.html)
- [io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html)
- A swappable version of [std::io](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/index.html)that works in`no_std + alloc`environments. If the feature flag`std`is enabled (as it is by default), this will just re-export types from`std::io`.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- The collection of traits and types you’ll likely need when working with binread and are unlikely to cause name conflicts.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A module for `Punctuated<T, P>``P`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A wrapper type for representing a layer of indirection within a file.
- [Null](https://docs.rs/struct.NullString.html)- String
- A null terminated UTF-8 string designed to make reading any null-terminated data easier.
- [Null](https://docs.rs/struct.NullWideString.html)- Wide - String
- A null terminated UTF-16 string designed to make reading any 16 bit wide null-terminated data easier.

- A wrapper where the position it was read from is stored alongside the value

- Runtime-configured options for reading the type using `BinRead`

# byteorder - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/byteorder/^1.5.0/

## Expand description

This crate provides convenience methods for encoding and decoding numbers in
either [big-endian or little-endian order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endianness).

The organization of the crate is pretty simple. A trait, [ ByteOrder](https://docs.rs/trait.ByteOrder.html), specifies
byte conversion methods for each type of number in Rust (sans numbers that have
a platform dependent size like

`usize` and `isize`). Two types, [and](https://docs.rs/enum.BigEndian.html)

`BigEndian`[implement these methods. Finally,](https://docs.rs/enum.LittleEndian.html)

`LittleEndian`[and](https://docs.rs/trait.ReadBytesExt.html)

`ReadBytesExt`[provide convenience methods available to all types that implement](https://docs.rs/trait.WriteBytesExt.html)

`WriteBytesExt`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Read.html)

`Read`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`Write`An alias, [ NetworkEndian](https://docs.rs/type.NetworkEndian.html), for

[is provided to help improve code clarity.](https://docs.rs/enum.BigEndian.html)

`BigEndian`An additional alias, [ NativeEndian](https://docs.rs/type.NativeEndian.html), is provided for the endianness of the
local platform. This is convenient when serializing data for use and
conversions are not desired.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Read unsigned 16 bit big-endian integers from a [ Read](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Read.html) type:

```
use std::io::Cursor;
use byteorder::{BigEndian, ReadBytesExt};
let mut rdr = Cursor::new(vec![2, 5, 3, 0]);
// Note that we use type parameters to indicate which kind of byte order
// we want!
assert_eq!(517, rdr.read_u16::<BigEndian>().unwrap());
assert_eq!(768, rdr.read_u16::<BigEndian>().unwrap());
```
Write unsigned 16 bit little-endian integers to a [ Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html) type:

```
use byteorder::{LittleEndian, WriteBytesExt};
let mut wtr = vec![];
wtr.write_u16::<LittleEndian>(517).unwrap();
wtr.write_u16::<LittleEndian>(768).unwrap();
assert_eq!(wtr, vec![5, 2, 0, 3]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional Features

This crate optionally provides support for 128 bit values (`i128` and `u128`)
when built with the `i128` feature enabled.

This crate can also be used without the standard library.

[§](https://docs.rs#alternatives)Alternatives

Note that as of Rust 1.32, the standard numeric types provide built-in methods
like `to_le_bytes` and `from_le_bytes`, which support some of the same use
cases.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [BigEndian](https://docs.rs/enum.BigEndian.html)
- Defines big-endian serialization.
- [Little](https://docs.rs/enum.LittleEndian.html)- Endian
- Defines little-endian serialization.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Byte](https://docs.rs/trait.ByteOrder.html)- Order
- `ByteOrder`describes types that can serialize integers as bytes.
- [Read](https://docs.rs/trait.ReadBytesExt.html)- Bytes - Ext
- Extends `Read``std::io`.)
- [Write](https://docs.rs/trait.WriteBytesExt.html)- Bytes - Ext
- Extends `Write``std::io`.)

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [BE](https://docs.rs/type.BE.html)
- A type alias for `BigEndian`
- [LE](https://docs.rs/type.LE.html)
- A type alias for `LittleEndian`
- [Native](https://docs.rs/type.NativeEndian.html)- Endian
- Defines system native-endian serialization.
- [Network](https://docs.rs/type.NetworkEndian.html)- Endian
- Defines network byte order serialization.

# hex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hex/^0.4.3/

## Expand description

Encoding and decoding hex strings.

For most cases, you can simply use the [ decode](https://docs.rs/fn.decode.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.encode.html)

`encode`[functions. If you need a bit more control, use the traits](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_upper.html)

`encode_upper`[and](https://docs.rs/trait.ToHex.html)

`ToHex`[instead.](https://docs.rs/trait.FromHex.html)

`FromHex`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
let hex_string = hex::encode("Hello world!");
println!("{}", hex_string); // Prints "48656c6c6f20776f726c6421"
```

- `pub use crate::serde::`- [serialize_upper](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.serialize_upper.html);- `alloc`and- `serde`

# leb128 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/leb128/^0.2.5/

## Expand description

Read and write DWARF’s “Little Endian Base 128” (LEB128) variable length integer encoding.

The implementation is a direct translation of the psuedocode in the DWARF 4 standard’s appendix C.

Read and write signed integers:

```
use leb128;
let mut buf = [0; 1024];
// Write to anything that implements `std::io::Write`.
{
    let mut writable = &mut buf[..];
    leb128::write::signed(&mut writable, -12345).expect("Should write number");
}
// Read from anything that implements `std::io::Read`.
let mut readable = &buf[..];
let val = leb128::read::signed(&mut readable).expect("Should read number");
assert_eq!(val, -12345);
```
Or read and write unsigned integers:

```
use leb128;
let mut buf = [0; 1024];
{
    let mut writable = &mut buf[..];
    leb128::write::unsigned(&mut writable, 98765).expect("Should write number");
}
let mut readable = &buf[..];
let val = leb128::read::unsigned(&mut readable).expect("Should read number");
assert_eq!(val, 98765);
```

---

# num_bigint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-bigint/^0.4/

## Expand description

Big Integer Types for Rust

- A `BigUint`
- A `BigInt``BigUint``Sign`

Common numerical operations are overloaded, so we can treat them the same way we treat other numbers.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_bigint::BigUint;
use num_traits::One;
// Calculate large fibonacci numbers.
fn fib(n: usize) -> BigUint {
    let mut f0 = BigUint::ZERO;
    let mut f1 = BigUint::ONE;
    for _ in 0..n {
        let f2 = f0 + &f1;
        f0 = f1;
        f1 = f2;
    }
    f0
}
// This is a very large number.
println!("fib(1000) = {}", fib(1000));
```
It’s easy to generate large random numbers:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use num_bigint::{ToBigInt, RandBigInt};
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let a = rng.gen_bigint(1000);
let low = -10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let high = 10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let b = rng.gen_bigint_range(&low, &high);
// Probably an even larger number.
println!("{}", a * b);
```
See the “Features” section for instructions for enabling random number generation.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

The `std` crate feature is enabled by default, which enables [ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html)
implementations and some internal use of floating point approximations. This can be disabled by
depending on

`num-bigint` with `default-features = false`. Either way, the `alloc` crate is
always required for heap allocation of the [/](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[digits.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#random-generation)Random Generation

`num-bigint` supports the generation of random big integers when the `rand`
feature is enabled. To enable it include rand as

```
rand = "0.8"
num-bigint = { version = "0.4", features = ["rand"] }
```
Note that you must use the version of `rand` that `num-bigint` is compatible
with: `0.8`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arbitrary-big-integers)Arbitrary Big Integers

`num-bigint` supports `arbitrary` and `quickcheck` features to implement
[ arbitrary::Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/1.4.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html) and

[, respectively, for both](https://docs.rs/quickcheck/1.0.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/quickcheck/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`quickcheck::Arbitrary`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[. These are useful for fuzzing and other forms of randomized testing.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

The `serde` feature adds implementations of [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) and

[for both](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[. Their serialized data is generated portably, regardless of platform differences like the internal digit size.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

The `num-bigint` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)
- A big signed integer type.
- [BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)
- A big unsigned integer type.
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/struct.ParseBigIntError.html)- BigInt - Error
- [Random](https://docs.rs/struct.RandomBits.html)- Bits - `rand`
- A random distribution for `BigUint``BigInt`
- [TryFrom](https://docs.rs/struct.TryFromBigIntError.html)- BigInt - Error
- The error type returned when a checked conversion regarding big integer fails.
- [U32Digits](https://docs.rs/struct.U32Digits.html)
- An iterator of `u32`digits representation of a`BigUint``BigInt`
- [U64Digits](https://docs.rs/struct.U64Digits.html)
- An iterator of `u64`digits representation of a`BigUint``BigInt`
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformBigInt.html)- BigInt - `rand`
- The back-end implementing rand’s `UniformSampler``BigInt`
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformBigUint.html)- BigUint - `rand`
- The back-end implementing rand’s `UniformSampler``BigUint`

- The trait for `NumAssign`types which also implement assignment operations taking the second operand by reference.
- [NumOps](https://docs.rs/trait.NumOps.html)
- Generic trait for types implementing basic numeric operations
- [NumRef](https://docs.rs/trait.NumRef.html)
- The trait for `Num`types which also implement numeric operations taking the second operand by reference.
- [RefNum](https://docs.rs/trait.RefNum.html)
- The trait for `Num`references which implement numeric operations, taking the second operand either by value or by reference.
